findings.description: The RDS instance sets storage_encrypted = false, so the database volume, snapshots and logs are stored unencrypted and no customer-managed KMS key is used.
publicly_accessible = true assigns the MySQL instance a public endpoint, exposing the database directly to the internet and relying solely on the security group and password for protection.
The master user is the default name 'admin', which makes credential guessing/brute-force easier on a publicly reachable instance.
No enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports (audit, error, general, slowquery) is configured, so security-relevant database events are not retained for investigation.
The RDS security group permits all outbound protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, providing an unrestricted data-exfiltration and command-and-control path.

The instance role grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*", allowing the EC2 instance (and anyone who compromises it) to read/modify all buckets, databases and network configuration in the account — a clear privilege-escalation path.
The database master password (var.password) is interpolated into the instance user_data script, which is readable by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute and via the instance metadata service.

No metadata_options block with http_tokens = "required" is set, so the legacy unauthenticated instance metadata service remains available; an SSRF in the PHP application would let an attacker steal the highly privileged role credentials.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance volume containing the credentials file dbinfo.inc may be stored unencrypted.

The instance is launched into a subnet that assigns a public DNS/IP (exported as output) and serves the application over plain HTTP with no TLS termination, so credentials and data submitted through the form travel unencrypted.
